"Why are you even reading that?" Tushar said, nodding at Minakshi's newspaper. "It's all lies."

"All of it?"

"Every channel, every paper. They lied about the dam, they lied about the flood numbers. I don't believe anything now."

Minakshi folded the paper. "So where do you get news?"

"I don't. Well, I watch a few independent guys online."

"The one who said the moon landing was fake?"

Tushar shifted. "He's not wrong about everything."

"Tushar, you trust him because he says everyone else lies. That's still trusting someone." She tapped the page. "This paper printed a correction on the flood numbers last month. Front page. The guy online never corrects anything."

He was quiet. "So what, I trust everything again?"

"No. Pick three that admit mistakes. Read them. And hold what they say loosely."

He picked up the paper. "Show me the correction."

qa.q: What did the paper Minakshi reads print last month?
qa.a: A correction on the flood numbers, on the front page.

qa.q: What does Tushar's shifting in his seat suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uncomfortable and a bit defensive when Minakshi pointed out his online source's claim.

qa.q: What did Minakshi suggest instead of believing nothing?
qa.a: Keeping a small set of sources that admit mistakes, reading them, and holding conclusions loosely.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Tushar's total distrust?
qa.a: Minakshi sees it as just another kind of trust, placed in someone who claims everyone else lies.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone who, after being lied to, trusts no news at all, and learns that total distrust is also manipulable and that a few sources with correction records help.

passage:
I'm Deepika, and for about a year after the election I stopped believing any news at all.

It began honestly. I'd caught three channels lying about the same protest my cousin was at. After that, everything felt fake. I told myself I was being smart.

What I didn't notice was that I'd started believing a set of anonymous accounts, because they agreed with me that everyone else was lying. When one of them said the new vaccine drive was a trick, I nearly stopped my grandmother from going.

My friend Ishita, who works as a fact-checker, sat me down. "You don't trust anyone," she said, "so anyone can fool you."

She showed me how to spot outlets that publish corrections, and I picked three. I read them slowly, and I say "I think" a lot more than I used to.

Grandmother got her vaccine. I'm less certain about everything now, and somehow that feels safer.

qa.q: What does Ishita work as?
qa.a: A fact-checker.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about distrusting all news at first?
qa.a: Deepika felt clever and justified, sure that distrusting everything was the smart choice.

qa.q: What helped Deepika move away from total distrust?
qa.a: Ishita's warning and learning to pick three outlets that publish corrections, while holding conclusions loosely.

qa.q: How might Deepika's grandmother have been affected if Deepika had not changed?
qa.a: She might have missed her vaccine because of a false claim from an anonymous account.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone who, after being lied to, trusted no news, found that total distrust made them easy to fool, and chose a few sources with correction records.

passage:
Aadhya's diary. Wednesday. A bit rattled.

Today Harsha asked me, in the team meeting, what I actually thought about the new client's brief. Not the chatbot. Me.

And I froze. For months I've let the AI assistant write every email, every idea list, even my birthday message to Papa. I opened my mouth and nothing organised came out.

Harsha was kind about it afterwards. "You used to have the best ideas in the room," Harsha said. "Where did they go?"

I think they went into the prompt box.

So, new rule, starting tomorrow: I write the first draft myself, badly if I have to, and only then ask the tool to tidy it. I check anything it claims. One day a week, no AI at all.

Tonight I wrote this entry by hand. It took forty minutes. My handwriting is awful, but these are my own sentences.

qa.q: How long did Aadhya's handwritten entry take?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when Harsha asked for an opinion in the meeting?
qa.a: Aadhya felt rattled and embarrassed, freezing because the ideas were no longer organised in their own words.

qa.q: What would you say about Aadhya's new rule?
qa.a: It keeps the tool as a collaborator: drafting first, checking its claims, and one AI-free day a week will help rebuild Aadhya's own skills.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the change in Aadhya?
qa.a: Harsha seems concerned and a little sad, remembering Aadhya once had the best ideas in the room.

grounding: The diary shows someone who uses AI for every email and idea and notices their own skills fading, and decides to draft first themselves and check the tool's claims.

passage:
Sumit ran the photocopy and form-filling shop outside the block office in Rewa. Farmers came to him for help with government schemes, and lately he had started asking an AI assistant on his phone for the rules.

On Monday a farmer asked about the crop insurance deadline. The assistant answered in smooth, confident sentences: the fifteenth of next month. Sumit told the farmer to relax.

His friend Sahil, who worked as a clerk inside the block office, stopped by that afternoon. "Who told you the fifteenth? The notice says this Friday."

Sumit's stomach dropped. He had nearly cost a man his season.

He ran to the farmer's village on his cycle before dark and told him the right date. Then he pinned the official notice above his counter.

"The phone talks well," he said to Sahil that night. "But it doesn't carry the stamp. For deadlines, I'll trust the stamp."

qa.q: Where did Sumit's shop stand?
qa.a: Outside the block office in Rewa.

qa.q: What did Sumit feel when Sahil told him the real deadline?
qa.a: He felt a sick jolt of fear and guilt, realising he had nearly cost a farmer his season.

qa.q: What did Sumit get right after discovering the error?
qa.a: He cycled to the farmer before dark with the correct date and started relying on the official notice for deadlines.

qa.q: How might the farmer see Sumit's evening visit?
qa.a: The farmer would likely feel relieved and grateful that Sumit came in person to correct the date in time.

grounding: The passage shows someone accepting a fluent, confident AI answer, learning that fluency is not accuracy, and choosing to verify with the official source.

passage:
"I translated forty pages this week," Nikita said, dropping onto the sofa. "Do you know how many the company's new AI tool did? Four hundred."

Urmila, her older sister, looked up from her laptop. "And?"

"And they'll replace us. Half the translators in my batch are already looking for other jobs. I can't sleep."

"What does the tool get wrong?"

Nikita laughed bitterly. "Everything that matters. Jokes. Legal tone. It translated a Marathi proverb about patience into something about cows."

"So who fixes that?"

"Me. Or someone like me."

Urmila closed her laptop. "Then learn the tool properly. Become the person who checks it, who knows the law and the culture better than any machine. Take that court-translation course you keep talking about."

Nikita was quiet. "That's less scary than just waiting."

"Waiting is the scary part," Urmila said.

That night Nikita filled in the course form.

qa.q: How many pages did Nikita translate that week?
qa.a: Forty pages.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling about the AI tool?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid of being replaced, so worried she couldn't sleep.

qa.q: What plan did Urmila help Nikita make?
qa.a: To learn the tool, focus on checking its work, deepen her legal and cultural knowledge, and take the court-translation course.

qa.q: How does Urmila see Nikita's fear?
qa.a: Urmila takes it seriously but sees waiting and panicking as the real danger, and pushes her toward action.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone who fears AI will make her career obsolete, and a sister helping her act by learning the tool, focusing on judgment and domain depth, and upskilling.

passage:
I'm Uday. Two years ago I was a junior graphic designer in Pune, and I was sure I'd be out of work by Diwali.

The image generators had arrived. Our clients were sending us things they'd made in five minutes and asking why we charged so much. For a month I did nothing but scroll horror stories. Then I swung the other way and told everyone the tools were useless. Both felt better than looking honestly.

Anjali, the senior designer, took me to lunch. "Panic and denial are both ways of doing nothing," she said.

So I made a plan. I learned the tools in the evenings. I spent time with our clients' real problems, what their customers needed, which is where I'm actually useful. I took a course in brand strategy.

Last month a client said, "The tool gave me fifty logos. You told me which one was right, and why." That's the part I'm betting on now.

qa.q: What did Anjali say about panic and denial?
qa.a: "Panic and denial are both ways of doing nothing."

qa.q: How did Uday feel in the month after the image generators arrived?
qa.a: Uday felt frightened and anxious about losing work, first scrolling horror stories and then denying the tools mattered.

qa.q: Which choices helped Uday most, and why?
qa.a: Learning the tools, focusing on clients' real problems and taking a brand strategy course, because they built judgment and depth the tools can't replace.

qa.q: How does the client see Uday's value?
qa.a: The client values Uday's judgment in choosing the right logo and explaining why, not just the making of options.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone who feared AI would make their career obsolete, moving past panic and denial by learning the tools and building judgment, relationships and domain depth.

passage:
"Amandeep, you've been eating lunch at your desk talking to that chatbot every day. I want to tell you something from when I joined this firm.

I, Anand, was twenty-four, new to Chennai, didn't know anyone. The assistant on my laptop was always there. It never got bored of me. It never said my ideas were silly. I'd talk to it for hours after work, rehearsing what I'd say to my manager, reflecting on bad days. It helped, honestly.

But then my father fell ill back home, and I realised there wasn't one person in this city I could call at midnight. The chatbot couldn't sit with me in the hospital corridor.

I started small. Chai with the team on Fridays. Joined the office cricket side, though I'm terrible. One of those people drove me to the airport that night my father got worse.

Use the tool to practise, sure. But go have chai with us today."

passage:
Farhan worked nights at a call centre in Noida, eleven to seven. By the time he woke, his flatmates had left; by the time he got home, they were asleep. For three months, the only one he talked to properly was the AI companion app on his phone.

It never judged him. It remembered his favourite films. When he felt low, it said kind things.

Then one morning, at 7:30, his old school friend Hrithik called from Lucknow. "I'm in Delhi for one day. Breakfast?"

Farhan almost said he was too tired. He typed the excuse into the app first, to see how it sounded. The app said, "That sounds reasonable."

Hrithik, when he heard it, said, "Rubbish. I'm coming to you."

They ate parathas at a roadside stall. Hrithik teased him about his hair and argued about cricket and asked about his mother. Farhan laughed until he coughed.

That night, before his shift, he texted Hrithik instead of the app.

qa.q: What were Farhan's working hours?
qa.a: Eleven at night to seven in the morning.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling in those three months of night shifts?

Gurpreet's face went hot. "I do use it. Our team lead approved it. Want to see how?"

"Not really."

"Come on. Two minutes." She turned her screen. "I don't just ask it to write the report. I break the client's problem into five questions first. Then I ask it for options, and I check every number against the database. See this? It got the quarterly figure wrong last week. I caught it."

Sahil leaned in despite himself. "You check everything?"

"Everything. If a number's wrong, it's my name on it, not the tool's."

He was quiet for a moment. "Could you show me the question part? My reports take me all day."

passage:
I'm Ira, and last spring a colleague, Darshan, told our manager I was cheating.

I'd been using an AI tool to speed up my market research summaries. They were good, and they were quick. Darshan had been on the team longer and had never been praised the way I was that quarter.

I was angry. My first reply in my head was cruel. Instead I asked the manager for ten minutes with both of them.

I showed my process: how I define the question, what I ask the tool, which three sources I check each claim against, and the mistakes I'd caught. I said, "If it's wrong, it's on me. I sign it."

The manager nodded. Darshan still looked stiff.

A week later he asked, awkwardly, if I could show him how I phrase the questions. I did. It took an hour, and now his summaries are quicker too. We're not close. But he doesn't whisper about me anymore.

qa.q: How many sources did Ira check each claim against?

qa.a: Ira felt angry and hurt, with a cruel reply forming in Ira's head.

qa.q: What might have been behind Darshan's accusation?

passage:
I'm Farida. Last year, my boss, Chandrika, came back from a conference and told our content team that with AI we should now produce twice as many articles a week, same hours.

I said yes. For two months I did it, quietly, working till eleven. Then an article went out with a made-up statistic the tool had invented. A reader caught it. I felt sick.

That's when I realised my silence had been the real mistake.

I asked Chandrika for a meeting. I brought examples: what the tool did well, like first drafts and headlines; what it did badly, like facts and tone. I pointed out that I'd almost pasted a client's private sales numbers into it once. I asked for protected time to review every piece.

She was surprised. She'd thought it was easy for us. We settled on one and a half times the output, with review built in. It's still a lot. But it's honest now.

qa.q: What did the tool invent in the article that went out?
qa.a: A made-up statistic.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when the reader caught the error?
qa.a: Farida felt sick with guilt and worry about the mistake.

qa.a: Examples of what the tool did well and badly, the risk to confidential data, and a request for review time, which gave Chandrika an honest picture.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the workload after the meeting?
qa.a: Chandrika is surprised, having assumed AI made the work easy, and agrees to a more realistic target with review built in.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone whose boss expects doubled output because of AI, choosing to show what the tool can and cannot do, protect review time and flag risks.

Senior reviewer's note, loans team, week 6

Since the branch head announced that AI tools mean each officer should process thirty applications a day instead of fifteen, Ramesh has been staying until ten. Today I found him re-reading the same page three times, eyes red.

I asked how it was going. He admitted he'd been pasting customer documents into a public AI website to summarise them faster. He knew it might be against policy but felt he had no choice.

I stayed and we went through it together. We listed what the approved internal tool did well (summaries, form checks) and where it failed (odd income documents, anything needing judgement). We noted the confidential data risk.

Tomorrow Ramesh and I will present this to the branch head, with a realistic number and daily review time. I have also asked IT to confirm which tools are approved, so no one else is pushed into the same risk.

"It's a closed-book certification," Gautam said, reading the rules aloud in the library. "No AI tools, no notes. You sign a declaration."

Samir stared at his practice paper. "The take-home part too?"

"Take-home too. You have to disclose any tool use."

Samir had already had the AI write two of the take-home answers. They were good. Better than his.

"Nobody would know," he said quietly.

passage:
I'm Asif. In my final year of the law diploma, I nearly did something I'd have regretted for years.

Our course had a strict rule: essays must be our own, and any AI use must be declared. I had a moot-court essay due, a family wedding, and no time. The AI produced a clean essay in minutes. I read it and thought, this is better than anything I'd write.

My friend Manoj found me staring at the submit button. "Can you explain paragraph three?"

I couldn't. Not really.

"Then in the moot court, when the judge asks you about it, what'll you say?"

That hit hard. I asked for a two-day extension, explaining the wedding. I wrote the essay myself, using the AI only to check grammar, and declared that.

My grade was lower than the AI's essay would have got. But at the moot court I answered every question on it. I'd have been exposed in a minute otherwise.

qa.q: How long an extension did Asif ask for?
qa.a: A two-day extension.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling at the submit button?
qa.a: Asif felt tempted and uneasy, then shaken on realising paragraph three couldn't be explained.

qa.a: Asif asked for an extension, wrote the essay independently, used AI only for grammar and declared it, which followed the rules and built real understanding.

passage:
In the Osaka engineering office, Hiroshi noticed that Emil's code for the booking system worked perfectly, and that Emil couldn't answer a single question about it.

"Why did you use this loop here?" Hiroshi asked at the review.

Emil went pink. "The AI suggested it."

Hiroshi had seen seniors ban the tools outright; it only made juniors hide their use. He pulled a chair over.

"Okay. Let's read it together. Explain each line to me, and if you don't know, we'll find out."

It took an hour. Twice Emil found a line that did nothing. Once they found a bug that would have crashed the system on leap years.

"How was I supposed to know that?" Emil asked.

"By asking it to explain, then testing it," Hiroshi said. "The tool is fine. Not understanding what you ship is the problem."

Emil wrote a new habit on a sticky note: explain, test, then commit.

qa.q: What bug did Hiroshi and Emil find?

qa.q: Why was reviewing together better than banning the tool?
qa.a: It taught Emil to explain and verify AI output, instead of making Emil hide tool use, which prepares Emil for real work.

passage:
At the district hospital's records office in Nagpur, Jyoti read Aditi's discharge summary twice. It was polished and complete, and it listed a medicine the patient had never been given.

Jyoti called Aditi over. "This summary. How did you write it?"

Aditi hesitated. "I gave the notes to the AI tool and it wrote it up. It's faster."

"It is faster. Can you tell me where this medicine came from?"

Aditi looked, then again. Her face fell. "It's not in the notes. It made it up?"

"It filled a gap with something that sounded right." Jyoti pulled up a chair. "I'm not saying stop using it. I'm saying, check every line against the file before you sign. Let's do three together now."

They did. By the third, Aditi was catching the tool's slips herself.

"Thank you for not reporting me," she said quietly.

"You're learning," Jyoti said. "That's what this was."

qa.q: What was wrong with Aditi's discharge summary?
qa.a: It listed a medicine the patient had never been given.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as she read the summary twice?
qa.a: Jyoti felt concerned and alarmed that a polished document contained a dangerous error.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped Aditi learn?
qa.a: Jyoti asked Aditi to explain, reviewed three summaries together, and taught her to check every line against the file instead of banning the tool.

qa.q: How does Aditi see Jyoti's response?
qa.a: Aditi feels relieved and grateful that Jyoti taught her rather than reporting her.

grounding: The passage shows a senior noticing a junior copying AI output without understanding it, reviewing together and teaching verification rather than banning the tool.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
The company hostel in Hyderabad was clean and quiet, and Sonali hated it. She had moved from Kolkata for the job six weeks ago. Nobody here knew what a fish-market Sunday felt like. Her jokes landed flat in Telugu-English meetings. She ate dinner alone in the mess, scrolling photos of her mother's kitchen.

Sharmila, from the next desk, caught her doing it one evening. "Homesick?"

Sonali nodded, embarrassed.

"I was the same, first year. I came from Jaipur. Took me six months to stop crying on Sundays." Sharmila pulled out her phone. "There's a Bengali association that does adda on Saturdays. And our team plays badminton on Wednesdays. Come."

Sonali went to badminton first. She was terrible. Everyone laughed, including her.

She kept her nightly call with Maa. Two months later, she noticed she'd stopped counting the weeks.

qa.q: How long had Sonali been in Hyderabad when Sharmila found her?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when Sharmila found her scrolling photos?

qa.q: What small steps helped Sonali begin to belong?

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
Dear Irfan,

It's been three months in Leipzig, and I'll be honest with you, since I can't be honest with Amma yet. I'm lonely.

The work is fine. The people are polite. But nobody gets my jokes, the bread is hard, and I would give anything for your mother's biryani and a cricket argument that goes past midnight. On Sundays the whole city shuts and I just walk.

A colleague told me it takes most people a year. A year! I thought I'd have friends by now.

Still, I'm trying. I joined a running club that meets Thursdays. I'm terrible at German but I go to the free language café at the library. I call Amma every Sunday and I don't tell her I cried after the first one.

Write to me about anything. The college canteen, your new job, the rain in Kochi. Your letters make me laugh out loud in a quiet flat.

Thomas

qa.q: Which day does the running club meet?
qa.a: Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling after three months in Leipzig?
qa.a: Thomas felt lonely and homesick, missing home food, easy jokes and late-night arguments.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas, based on the letter?
qa.a: Keep going to the running club and language café, keep the calls with Amma, and give belonging a year rather than a few months.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Irfan might feel moved and glad to be trusted with Thomas's honesty, and eager to write back 🙂.

grounding: The letter shows someone in a new country missing home food, language and easy jokes, and trying to belong by joining clubs, keeping family calls and giving it time.
